statements: The chief complaint is 3 days of upper abdominal pain in a previously healthy 26-year-old man.
The initial bedside concern appears to have been an acute surgical abdomen or biliary disease.
He had epigastric tenderness with rebound.
He had a positive Murphy’s sign.
CT showed a hyperdense gallbladder with mild wall swelling.
The patient was afebrile.
Procalcitonin was normal.
CRP was normal.
Imaging showed multisystem fluid accumulation in the chest, pericardial sac, and abdomen.
Salient positive findings are upper abdominal pain.
Salient positive findings are epigastric tenderness with rebound.
Salient positive findings are a positive Murphy’s sign.
Salient positive findings are mild jaundice.
Salient positive findings are a mildly elevated leukocyte count.
CT showed mild gallbladder wall swelling.
CT showed fluid in pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal spaces.
ECG showed ST-segment depression.
ECG showed T-wave inversion in V1–4.
ECG showed prolonged QT.
At laparotomy, there was ascites.
At laparotomy, there was bowel wall edema.
At laparotomy, there was no bowel perforation.
At laparotomy, there was no gallbladder enlargement.
At laparotomy, there was no cholangitis.
The operative finding of about 1000 mL peritoneal fluid strongly suggests a systemic capillary leak or third-spacing process rather than a focal intra-abdominal infection.
The operative finding of bowel wall edema strongly suggests a systemic capillary leak or third-spacing process rather than a focal intra-abdominal infection.
He had no history of hypertension.
He had no history of heart disease.
He was afebrile.
Procalcitonin was normal.
CRP was normal.
These findings argue against acute bacterial cholecystitis, cholangitis, or perforated viscus.
Intraoperatively there was no bowel perforation.
Intraoperatively there was no gallbladder enlargement.
Intraoperatively there was no cholangitis.
These intraoperative findings directly refute the presumed surgical biliary diagnosis.
The presence of pericardial fluid is atypical for isolated gallbladder disease.
The presence of pleural fluid is atypical for isolated gallbladder disease.
The first differential is acute cholecystitis or cholangitis.
The reason for that differential is the positive Murphy’s sign, mild jaundice, leukocytosis, and gallbladder wall changes on CT.
This differential becomes less likely because the patient was afebrile.
This differential becomes less likely because inflammatory markers were normal.
This differential becomes less likely because surgery found no gallbladder enlargement or cholangitis.
Gallbladder wall edema can be secondary to systemic edema rather than primary gallbladder inflammation.
A second differential is perforated viscus or other surgical peritonitis.
The reason for that differential is rebound tenderness and ascites.
This differential becomes unlikely because laparotomy showed no perforation.
This differential becomes unlikely because laparotomy showed bowel wall edema and free fluid.
These findings favor a systemic process.
A third differential is acute pancreatitis.
The reason for that differential is that acute pancreatitis can cause epigastric pain, ascites, pleural effusions, and reactive gallbladder changes.
No pancreatic findings are provided.
No enzyme abnormalities are provided.
The ECG abnormalities are not typical core features of acute pancreatitis.
Pericardial effusion is not a typical core feature of acute pancreatitis.
A fourth and more fitting differential is a systemic capillary leak state.
This systemic capillary leak state would cause serosal effusions, bowel wall edema, gallbladder wall edema, and abdominal pain.

In a young patient with pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal effusions plus bowel wall edema and no evidence of infection or perforation, hereditary angioedema with gastrointestinal involvement is a strong fit.
Hereditary angioedema can present as severe abdominal pain mimicking an acute abdomen.
Hereditary angioedema can present with ascites.
Hereditary angioedema can present with bowel wall edema.
Hereditary angioedema can present with gallbladder wall edema.
Hereditary angioedema can present with pleural effusions due to increased vascular permeability.
Hereditary angioedema can present with pericardial effusions due to increased vascular permeability.
The ECG changes could reflect systemic illness or electrolyte effects.
The ECG changes could reflect myocardial involvement from the same process.
The key diagnostic pattern is unexplained multisystem edema and effusions with a negative laparotomy.

The combination of acute abdominal pain, bowel wall edema, large-volume ascites, pleural and pericardial effusions, mild gallbladder wall edema mimicking cholecystitis, and absence of infectious or surgical pathology most strongly supports hereditary angioedema presenting with an abdominal attack.
This diagnosis best unifies the false-positive Murphy’s sign, the imaging, and the negative exploratory laparotomy.
The high differential diagnosis is hereditary angioedema with abdominal attack.
The medium differential diagnosis is acute cholecystitis or cholangitis.
The low differential diagnosis is perforated viscus or generalized surgical peritonitis.
The low differential diagnosis is acute pancreatitis.
The final diagnosis is hereditary angioedema with abdominal attack.
